conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that regular intake of vitamin C does not prevent colds in the general population, citing systematic review evidence showing no meaningful reduction in cold incidence. Therefore, it rejects the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
## Does Regular Vitamin C Prevent Colds? — No, With One Exception

**Short answer: No.** For the general population, taking vitamin C regularly does not prevent colds. The evidence does, however, show modest benefits for cold duration/severity, and a notable exception for people under extreme physical stress.

**The evidence:**

The definitive source here is the Cochrane systematic review by Hemilä and colleagues, which pooled data from 29 trial comparisons involving over 11,000 participants on cold incidence. It found no meaningful reduction in the general population's likelihood of catching a cold with regular vitamin C supplementation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold). Other summaries of this Cochrane body of work reach the same conclusion — that "routine mega-dose prophylaxis is not rationally justified" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ebch.266) and that regular supplementation "won't protect most people from colds" (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/).

**Nuances worth noting:**
- **Duration/severity, not prevention:** The same Cochrane analysis found regular supplementation modestly shortens cold duration (~8% in adults, ~14% in children) once a cold occurs — a real but small effect, distinct from prevention (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/).
- **Exception for extreme exertion:** In a subset of trials involving marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers under heavy physical/cold stress, vitamin C roughly halved cold incidence (pooled RR ~0.50), suggesting a preventive effect only in this specific high-stress population (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/).
- Starting vitamin C after symptoms begin has no therapeutic effect (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/).

**Conclusion:** The "no" answer is well-supported for the general population; vitamin C is not a preventive strategy against colds for most people, though it modestly reduces cold duration and may help those under intense physical exertion.
